output.headline: Internal Reform inquiry clears Jukes and Orr over Farage's £5m gift
output.bodyHtml:
A parliamentary watchdog is still investigating whether the £5m gift Nigel Farage received from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.

Nigel Farage undermined his own claim that the gift was for security when he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.

The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.

The admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian, in which Dan Jukes said it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.

Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”

Previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has now revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.

The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.

After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”

The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”

“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”

The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.

Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”

If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.

Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.

Reform’s own internal investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations; a police investigation into the gift is continuing.

Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.

The timeline for the gift is disputed.

Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.

According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.

The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.

Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.

A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.

Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.

Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”

They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.
output.standfirst: Exclusive: an internal Reform investigation has cleared Dan Jukes and James Orr of breaking foreign donation laws, even as undercover footage of Jukes suggesting the £5m gift was a Brexit reward raises fresh questions and a parliamentary watchdog continues its own inquiry.
output.progress: A parliamentary watchdog is separately investigating whether the gift should have been declared, and a police investigation is also ongoing.

output.headline: Ministers draft bill to open path to public ownership of water firms
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.

One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.

One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.

“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.

Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.

Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.

Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.

Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.

When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.

Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.

Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.

Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.

While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.

Burnham is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.

Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”

The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.

Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.

Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.

“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”

Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.

“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Angela Eagle is working on a bill to ease public ownership of water firms, as Burnham pushes officials to go further for Thames Water, which recently asked creditors for a further £2.4bn as it struggles to stay afloat.
output.progress: Burnham has also told officials to look at bolder options, including taking a stake in Thames Water via unpaid environmental fines.

output.headline: Macron orders full security review and new tactics for French police
output.bodyHtml:
Partial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.

Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.

His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.

Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday in two areas in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place on Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.

A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.

France’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.

Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.

Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.

Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.

Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.

He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.

The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential election and amid mounting economic pressures.

Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said.

France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.

Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence,” he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.

Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 imprisoned since the violence broke out over the weekend, Libération reported.

Some 70% of those arrested were adults and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes have been injured.

Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.

Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.

“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”

Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.

On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.

A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”

In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.

Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.
output.standfirst: Partial curfews are in force in Lille and Paris as Macron orders new tactics and a review, after police 'lost control' of riots that brought 2,513 arrests and injured about 1,000 officers
output.progress: The justice ministry says about 80% of those arrested are being prosecuted, and platforms have been asked to remove listings for stolen goods.

output.headline: Drivers win guaranteed grace periods and scrapped fines for honest mistakes
output.bodyHtml:
New rules for private car parks will guarantee drivers five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends before they can be fined, in a change Andy Burnham said was designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges.

Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”

The prime minister said the new official code of practice for the industry — the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal — meant motorists in England, Scotland and Wales would enjoy a range of new rights.

New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”.

Fines will also be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine.

The government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal for “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration — though this appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”.

Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August, the RAC said the number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26.

Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation was passed in early 2019, and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then government in early 2022 – but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn.

In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”.

The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however.

The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code.

Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher.

On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether.
output.standfirst: New rules guarantee drivers five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave, with fines scrapped for honest mistakes — though Which? says they fall short of the £50 cap campaigners wanted.
output.progress: Andy Burnham is introducing a new code of practice guaranteeing grace periods and scrapping fines for honest mistakes, with a consultation on debt fees due next year.

output.headline: Court extends detention of West Bank settler-attack suspects after rare raid
output.bodyHtml:
Israeli police detained 10 people connected with a weekend of attacks on foreigners and the construction of an illegal outpost, releasing footage of a rare raid on settlers on Monday morning.

Hours later a court extended the detention of six of the men, to between three and four days.

The detentions followed a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank, including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.

She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.

“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.

The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.

He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.

There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.

“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.

Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.

“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.

Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.

Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.

His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.

Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.

Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.

Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.

It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.

Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.
output.standfirst: Six men suspected of attacking a US photojournalist and visiting European diplomats in the West Bank remain in custody, after Israeli police carried out a rare raid that led to 10 arrests.
output.progress: A court has extended the detention of six men linked to the attacks, after international condemnation from the US, Europe and media figures.

output.headline: A single photo could help guide cancer treatment, study finds
output.bodyHtml:
Doctors have built an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.

The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.

It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.

Details of the breakthrough were published in the Lancet Digital Health journal.

The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face, according to the results of a study that examined the model.

Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.

Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.

Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.

“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”

Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.

“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”

The results of the study suggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.

The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.

The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.

Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.

“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”

Researchers found lifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.

“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”

Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.
output.standfirst: Trained on more than 40 million facial photographs, the system estimates a person's biological age and could help doctors tailor cancer treatment, though researchers say more work is needed before wide use.
output.progress: Researchers say the tool needs further study before it could be used to support personalised treatment decisions.

output.headline: Police give journalist's family protection as Tommy Robinson faces trial
output.bodyHtml:
Andrew Young and his family were given a close protection officer, while Jacob Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner left their home, after what is alleged to have been a campaign of intimidation by the far-right activist Tommy Robinson.

Tommy Robinson, the far-right activist, deployed what a court has been told were “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” that forced journalists and their family members to flee their homes, as his harassment trial got under way.

Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, is alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats.

He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies.

Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark crown court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024.

The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.”

“This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt.

“On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes.

“That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers.

Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”.

Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about.

Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.”

When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house.

Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.”

The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues.

Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.”

A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children.

In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?”

The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.
output.standfirst: A close protection officer was assigned to one Mail Online reporter's family, as a court heard how Tommy Robinson's online posts allegedly drove two journalists from their homes amid threats, which he denies.
output.progress: The case opened at Southwark crown court on Monday, with prosecutor Ben Holt setting out two harassment charges against Robinson, which he denies.

output.headline: Engineers safely remove masts from sunken WWII bomb ship in the Thames
output.bodyHtml:
Engineers have made a sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary slightly safer, ministers have announced, reducing a risk from a wreck that holds enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London.

Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.

The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.

The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.

The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.

Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in a “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.

Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”

He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.

The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.

A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead.

Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.

output.headline: Mission to Phobos could reveal secrets of the solar system's origins, scientists say
output.bodyHtml:
Japan has successfully launched a spacecraft on an unprecedented mission to bring back samples from one of Mars’s moons that scientists hope will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.

The Martian ⁠Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft, propelled by Japan’s flagship H3 rocket, lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima island in the country’s far south-west, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) said.

The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars’s orbit in August next year and collect at least 10g of soil and rock from the surface of Phobos, one of two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting the planet. It is scheduled to return in 2031, Jaxa said.

Related: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests

The pock-marked moon, which has a diameter measuring 14 miles (22.5km), orbits Mars three times a day about 6,000km above its surface.

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the unmanned probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from Tanegashima Space Centre at 4:41am, witnessed by thousands of people who had woken up early to follow a livestream.

An hour later, Jaxa scientists declared the launch a success when the spacecraft separated from the rocket’s upper stage, prompting scenes of celebration in the flight control room.

Nasa has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past half a century, while China landed on the Martian surface in 2021, but this is the first time anyone has attempted to land on Phobos or the planet’s smaller moon, Deimos.

“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said Nasa astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the Japan-led project to collect samples.

Five space agencies are collaborating on the five-year mission, which will attempt to land a robotic prospector and a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons.

The $578m mission features a five-tonne spacecraft that will sync with Phobos’ tight orbit around Mars when it arrives next summer. It will then eject a small French-German rover, named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.

If all goes according to plan, the four-wheeled rover will bounce (due to gravity on Phobos being 1/1,000th as strong as Earth) for several minutes on Mars’s surface before coming to a halt. It will spend 100 days surveying the planet’s surface to find safe landing and sampling sites ahead of the arrival of the main craft, a four-legged stationary lander that will gather the samples.

The lander will spend only two hours on Phobos drilling and vacuuming up material, before launching back into space. Officials said it would observe Deimos during several flybys before leaving Mars’s orbit in November 2030.

“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the Germany Space Agency’s rover chief Markus Grebenstein.

Scientists hope the samples will help them establish how Phobos and Deimos were formed and even offer clues about the origins of life. MMX’s findings will also help shape future Mars missions, including crewed expeditions, Nasa said.

According to one theory – the “giant impact” hypothesis – the two moons formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. A second proposition, known as the “capture” hypothesis, suggests that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars’s gravity.

Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four planets closest to the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

The US and China are in a race to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars. Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples, but its return to Earth was halted by the Trump administration after a congressional vote in January this year.

China’s Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled to launch around 2028 and could bring back Mars samples as early as 2031, potentially before the Japanese moon mission’s return.
output.standfirst: Scientists hope samples gathered from Phobos will reveal how the moon formed and shed light on the origins of life, while the US and China race to bring back rock from Mars.
